Story · Lesson 1

Miss Huda's First Month

Huda got the job. Now she has to get used to early mornings and thirty children. Read the story, then read it from the head teacher's point of view.

Talk about past habits with used toSay what feels normal with be used toDescribe a change with get used to

1The story

Huda got the job. Two weeks after her interview with Mrs. Karim, she started work as a teaching assistant at a primary school in Omdurman. On her first morning, her alarm rang at five, and she almost threw her phone across the room. At university, she used to sleep until eight. Now she had to be at school before seven.

The first week was hard. Huda wasn't used to standing all day, and she wasn't used to the noise. When she tried to read the class a story, half of the thirty children talked, and the other half asked to go to the bathroom. By Thursday, she felt like a fish out of water. "Maybe I'm not made for this," she told Sara on the phone.

"Of course you are," said Sara. "You used to be shy, remember? You didn't use to speak in class at all. And now you're a teacher. Give it time."

In the second week, Huda watched Mrs. Karim carefully. She noticed that the head teacher never shouted. Instead, she clapped three times, and the room went quiet. Huda tried it. The first time, nobody listened. The fifth time, half the class clapped back. By the end of the week, everyone did.

Slowly, Huda got used to the early mornings. She got used to eating her breakfast in two minutes and answering forty questions an hour. She even began to get the hang of the old photocopier, which jammed every time someone looked at it.

On the last day of her first month, a small boy called Yassin, who used to hide under his desk, stood up and read a whole page aloud. When he finished, the class clapped. Huda had to look out of the window for a moment.

That evening, she called Sara again. "I'm finally used to it," she said. "Well, almost." Sara laughed. "See? Rome wasn't built in a day."

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1

2

3
Until what time did she use to sleep at university?Until eight.
4
What wasn't she used to in the first week?Standing all day, and the noise.
5
How did she feel by Thursday?Like a fish out of water.
6
What did Sara remind her?That she used to be shy and didn't use to speak in class.
7
What did Mrs. Karim do instead of shouting?She clapped three times.
8
What happened the fifth time Huda clapped?Half the class clapped back.
9
What did Huda slowly get used to?The early mornings, eating breakfast in two minutes, and answering forty questions an hour.
10
What was wrong with the photocopier?It jammed every time someone looked at it.
11
What did Yassin use to do?Hide under his desk.
12
What did Yassin do on the last day of the month?He stood up and read a whole page aloud.

3Point of view Now Mrs. Karim tells it.

MK

When Huda started at our school, I could see that she wasn't used to young children. Her voice was too quiet, and she was used to students who listened. In her first week, the class didn't hear a word she said.

But she watched and learned. She noticed that I never shout, and she started to clap like me. Teachers used to shout a lot when I was young, but I have never believed in it.

By the end of the month, she had gotten used to everything, the noise, the early mornings, and even our terrible photocopier.

I knew she would be a good teacher on the day Yassin read aloud. That boy used to hide under his desk, and Huda had sat with him every day for a month. I think they are both a little braver now.

4What did you learn?

You learned used to, be used to, and get used to.

They look similar, but they mean different things. Used to is about the past. Be used to and get used to are about what feels normal.

FormMeaningExample
used to + verba habit in the past, not nowShe used to sleep until eight.
didn't use to + verbnot a habit in the pastShe didn't use to speak in class.
be used to + noun / -ingit feels normal nowShe is used to the noise now.
get used to + noun / -ingit is becoming normalShe got used to getting up early.
used to has no presentFor now, say: I usually get up at five. Not: I use to get up.
After be / get used to: -ingI'm used to getting up early. Not: I'm used to get up.
Say it: yoost-tuhIn used to, the s sounds like s, not z.
QuestionsWhat did you use to do as a child that you don't do now?I used to play football every afternoon.

phraseget the hang of something

to learn how to do something, usually after some practice

Driving was difficult at first, but I soon got the hang of it.
proverbRome wasn't built in a day.

Important things take time, so be patient.

You won't speak perfect English in a month. Rome wasn't built in a day.

clappedhit your hands together to make a noise
photocopiera machine that makes copies of papers
jammedgot stuck and stopped working
aloudin a voice that other people can hear
braverless afraid than before

Topic · Lesson 2

Life Before Smartphones

How people called, found their way, and kept in touch before the phone in your pocket, and what we have got used to.

Compare life then and nowUse used to and be used toTalk about technology in your life

1Read

Today, most of us check our phones more than fifty times a day, and it is hard to imagine life without them. But only twenty years ago, things were very different. How did people live before smartphones?

First, people used to remember things. Most people knew dozens of phone numbers by heart. To call someone, they used a landline, a phone connected to the wall. If nobody was home, they simply tried again later.

To find their way in a new city, people used paper maps, or they stopped and asked for directions. Getting lost was normal, and sometimes it led to an adventure.

To keep in touch with family in another country, people wrote letters, and a letter could take two or three weeks to arrive. A phone call abroad was so expensive that many families made one only once in a blue moon, on Eid or for very important news.

Photos were different too. A film camera could take only thirty-six pictures, and you didn't see them until they were printed in a shop. So people took photos of special moments only.

Today, we are used to answers in seconds, maps that speak, and video calls that cost nothing. Most of this is wonderful. But some experts say that we should sometimes put our phones away, because the people who lived before smartphones were better at one thing. They knew how to be bored.

2Then and now

Numbersthen remembered · now saved
Directionsthen paper maps · now GPS
Family abroadthen letters · now video calls
Photosthen 36 on a film · now thousands

4

5New words

Looking for an Apartment

Calling about an apartment to rent

Ask about an apartmentTalk about what you are used toAsk to visit before you decide

1Read the conversation

Adam wants to live closer to the flying school. He calls Mr. Hassan, who has an apartment to rent.
MHMR. HASSANHello, Hassan speaking.
AADAMHello. I'm calling about the apartment near the flying school. Is it still available?
MHMR. HASSANYes. It's a one-bedroom apartment on the second floor, with a small kitchen and a balcony. It's very quiet, too.
AADAMThat sounds good. I'm not used to living alone, so I'd like somewhere near shops. Is there a market nearby?
MHMR. HASSANThere's one five minutes away. The rent is paid monthly, but I ask for two months in advance.
AADAMTwo months in advance? Apartments near the school really cost an arm and a leg.
MHMR. HASSANI understand. But water is included, and the furniture is new. You won't need to buy anything.
AADAMThat helps. Can I come and see it before I decide?
MHMR. HASSANOf course. Come tomorrow at five. Then you can sleep on it and call me the next day.
AADAMPerfect. Thank you, Mr. Hassan. See you tomorrow.

2Useful phrases

Ask if it is free

Is it still available?

Say what you are used to

I'm not used to living alone.

Ask about the area

Is there a market nearby?

React to the price

Two months in advance?

Ask to visit

Can I come and see it before I decide?

End the call

Thank you. See you tomorrow.

Story · Lesson 4

The Road Not Taken

Thirty years ago, Mr. Ali said no to a job that would have made him rich. Read the story, then read it from the point of view of a girl in his class.

Imagine a different presentUse mixed conditionalsTalk about big decisions

1The story

Thirty years ago, Mr. Ali was in his first year as a teacher at a small school in Khartoum, and he loved it. Then one day, a letter arrived from a bank in Dubai. They were offering him a job as a translator, with a salary ten times bigger than his. He was at a crossroads.

His friends told him to go. His father told him to go. Even the head teacher said, "Ali, an offer like this won't come again."

But that week, a quiet girl in his class, who had never answered a question, put up her hand. "Teacher, what does future mean?" she asked. Mr. Ali explained, and he saw her face change. That night, he wrote to the bank and turned down the job.

Last week, his students asked him about it. "Do you ever wish you had gone?" asked Omar. Mr. Ali smiled. "Sometimes. If I had taken that job, I would be rich now. I would be living in a big apartment by the sea, and I would have a much nicer car."

"So why didn't you go?" asked Adam. "If I had gone to Dubai," said Mr. Ali, "I wouldn't know any of you. Huda wouldn't be a teacher, because nobody would have pushed her to apply. And that quiet girl? You know her. Her name is Dr. Amira Salih. She was a guest on your podcast."

The room went silent. Then Sara asked, "But don't you ever wonder?" "Of course," said Mr. Ali. "The grass is always greener on the other side. But when I look at my side, I see thirty years of students. If I were rich, I wouldn't be this happy."

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1

2

3

4

5
What did his friends and his father tell him?To go.
6
What did the quiet girl ask?What future means.
7
What did Mr. Ali do that night?He wrote to the bank and turned down the job.
8
What would he be now if he had taken the job?Rich.
9
Where would he be living?In a big apartment by the sea.
10
Why wouldn't Huda be a teacher?Because nobody would have pushed her to apply.
11
Who was the quiet girl?Dr. Amira Salih.
12
What does Mr. Ali see when he looks at his side?Thirty years of students.

3Point of view Now Dr. Amira tells it.

DA

When I was nine, I was the quietest girl in the class. I never answered a question, because I was afraid of being wrong.

Then one day, a young teacher wrote the word future on the board. I didn't know what it meant, and for the first time, I put up my hand. He explained it so kindly that I went home and told my mother I wanted to study the future. Today, that's my job.

Years later, I learned that he had a job offer in Dubai that same week, and he said no. If he had left, I might not be a scientist today. I might still be afraid of my own questions.

Last month, I visited his class to say thank you. He pretended that he didn't remember me. But he did.

4What did you learn?

You learned mixed conditionals.

We use them when a different past would change the present. The if part is about the past, and the result is about now.

A different pastA different now
If I had taken that job,I would be rich now.
If I had gone to Dubai,I wouldn't know any of you.
If he had left,I might not be a scientist today.
If I hadn't studied English,I wouldn't be a teacher.
If + had done, would + doIf I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
The other way: now and pastIf I were braver, I would have taken the job.
might or could for maybeShe might not be a scientist today.
QuestionsHow would your life be different if you had grown up in another country?If I had grown up in Japan, I would speak Japanese.

5Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idiombe at a crossroads

to be at a time when you must make an important decision

After school, I was at a crossroads. Should I work or go to university?
phraseturn down

to say no to an offer

She turned down the job because it was too far from home.
proverbThe grass is always greener on the other side.

Other people's lives always seem better than ours, even when they are not.

My friend wants my job, and I want his. The grass is always greener on the other side.

translatora person who changes words from one language into another
salarythe money you get every month for your job
applyask for a job or a place at a school in writing
silentwith no sound at all
wonderthink about something and want to know more
pretendedacted as if something was true when it was not

Science · Lesson 5

The Green Sahara

Thousands of years ago, the biggest hot desert in the world was full of lakes, rivers, and animals. What changed?

Explain how a place changed over timeTalk about evidence from the pastUse if with a different past and a different present

1Read

Today, the Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world. It covers most of North Africa, including much of northern Sudan. But about 10,000 years ago, it looked completely different. It was green.

Scientists call this time the African Humid Period. For thousands of years, heavy summer rains reached far into the desert. There were grasslands, trees, and huge lakes, and hippos, giraffes, and elephants lived where there is only sand today.

How do we know? The people who lived there left rock art, paintings and carvings on the rocks that show cattle, giraffes, and even people swimming. In Sudan, scientists have found that Wadi Howar, a dry valley in the northwest, was once a long river that carried water toward the Nile. Some call it the Yellow Nile. But the rock art and the old riverbeds are only the tip of the iceberg. Under the sand, there are old villages, tools, and fish bones.

So what changed? The answer is in space. The Earth slowly wobbles as it turns, like a spinning top. Over thousands of years, this changed how much summer sunlight reached North Africa. With less sunlight, the summer rains moved south, the lakes and rivers dried up, and about 5,000 years ago, the desert returned.

Many people moved toward the Nile, where there was still water. Some historians believe that if the Sahara had stayed green, life in the Nile Valley would be very different today. And the Earth is still wobbling, so in thousands of years, the Sahara may be green again.

2How the green Sahara became a desert

1Wobblethe Earth slowly tilts in a new way
2Less sunsummers in North Africa get weaker
3Less rainthe summer rains move south
4Desertlakes and rivers dry up
Did you know?

The Sahara is almost as big as the United States, but only about a quarter of it is sand. The rest is rock, stones, and mountains.

3Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1

2

3
What does the rock art show?Cattle, giraffes, and even people swimming.
4
What was Wadi Howar?A long river that carried water toward the Nile.
5
Why did the summer rains move south?The Earth's wobble changed how much summer sunlight reached North Africa.
6
When did the desert return?About 5,000 years ago.
7
Where did many people move?Toward the Nile, where there was still water.

phrasedry up

5New words

humidwith a lot of water in the air
carvingspictures cut into stone or wood

My Flight Has Been Canceled

Finding a solution at the airline desk

Explain a travel problemTalk about a different past and presentAsk for better options

1Read the conversation

Sara is at Khartoum airport. Her flight to Cairo has been canceled, and she is speaking at a conference there this afternoon. She goes to the airline desk.
AGAGENTGood morning. How can I help you?
SSARAGood morning. My flight to Cairo at ten has been canceled, and I'm speaking at a conference there this afternoon.
AGAGENTI'm very sorry. There's a problem with the plane. Everyone on that flight is in the same boat, I'm afraid.
SSARAIf I had booked the earlier flight, I would be in Cairo now. What are my options?
AGAGENTThere's a flight at four this afternoon, or one tomorrow at seven in the morning.
SSARAMy talk is at five, so four is too late. Is there anything earlier, on another airline?
AGAGENTLet me check. Yes, there's one seat on a flight at one. We'll pay for the change, and you'll get a meal voucher.
SSARAThat's wonderful. I'll arrive just in time.
AGAGENTLook on the bright side. If you hadn't come to the desk so early, that seat would be gone now.
SSARAThat's true. Thank you so much for your help.

2Useful phrases

Explain the problem

My flight has been canceled.

Say why it matters

I'm speaking at a conference this afternoon.

Imagine a different past

If I had booked the earlier flight, I would be in Cairo now.

Ask for options

What are my options?

Ask for something better

Is there anything earlier, on another airline?

Thank someone

Thank you so much for your help.

3Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idiombe in the same boat

to be in the same difficult situation as other people

Don't worry about the exam. We're all in the same boat.
phraselook on the bright side

to see the good part of a bad situation

You missed the bus, but look on the bright side. You got some exercise!

4New words

canceledstopped so that it will not happen
bookedpaid for a seat or a room before you use it
optionsthings you can choose from
airlinea company that flies planes for passengers
vouchera paper you can use instead of money
just in timeat the last moment, but not late

Story · Lesson 7

Omar's New Office

Omar wants a professional office in one week. He has the walls painted, a sign made, and the internet installed, and everything goes wrong. Read the story, then read it from Sara's point of view.

Say what other people do for youUse have and get something doneTell a funny story about a bad week

1The story

After a year at Dr. Idris's company, Omar finally started his own business, a small company that repairs phones and builds apps. He rented a room above a shop in the market and decided to make it look professional. "It'll be a piece of cake," he told Adam. "I'll have everything done in a week."

On Monday, he had the walls painted blue. When he came back in the evening, they were bright green. "Blue was finished," the painter explained. "Green is nicer."

On Tuesday, he got a sign made for the door. It said OMAR'S TECNOLOGY. "Where's the H?" Omar asked. "Letters are expensive," said the sign maker. "Nobody will notice."

On Wednesday, he had the internet installed. The man worked for three hours, drank four cups of tea, and left. The internet worked for exactly twenty minutes.

By Thursday, Omar was tired of waiting for other people. "If you want something done right, do it yourself," he said, and he bought a can of blue paint. Two hours later, the walls were blue and green, and so were Omar, the floor, and the window.

That evening, Sara came to see the office. She looked at the walls, the sign, and Omar's blue hair, and she tried not to laugh. "Maybe you just need the right people," she said. The next day, she called her cousin, a painter who never changed colors. Huda's brother got the sign fixed in an hour, and Adam's uncle had the internet checked by a friend who really knew what he was doing.

A week later, the office looked perfect. Omar sorted out the last problem himself, a door that wouldn't close, and he opened the business on Sunday. His first customer was Mr. Ali, who wanted to have his phone repaired. "Don't worry," Omar said. "I'll do this one myself."

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1

2

3
What did Omar tell Adam?That it would be a piece of cake, and he would have everything done in a week.
4
What color did Omar want the walls?Blue.
5
What color were they when he came back?Bright green.
6
What was wrong with the sign?The H was missing. It said TECNOLOGY.
7
How long did the internet work?For exactly twenty minutes.
8
What happened when Omar painted the walls himself?The walls were blue and green, and so were Omar, the floor, and the window.
9
What did Sara say?Maybe he just needed the right people.
10
Who got the sign fixed?Huda's brother.
11
What problem did Omar sort out himself?A door that wouldn't close.
12
Who was his first customer?Mr. Ali.

3Point of view Now Sara tells it.

S

Omar called me on Thursday night. "Come and see my office," he said. He sounded very tired.

When I arrived, the walls were blue and green, the sign on the door said TECNOLOGY, and Omar had blue paint in his hair. He told me that he had had the walls painted, got a sign made, and had the internet installed, and that everything had gone wrong.

So I made three phone calls. By Saturday, we had everything fixed by people who knew what they were doing.

Omar says that he learned a lesson about business that week. I think he learned a lesson about paint.

4What did you learn?

You learned the causative, have or get something done.

We use it when another person does a job for us. We say what was done, not who did it.

have / get + thing + past participleWhat it means
He had the walls painted.A painter painted them for him.
He got a sign made.Someone made it for him.
He had the internet installed.A technician installed it.
I want to have my phone repaired.I want someone to repair it.
get is less formalI got my hair cut. I had my hair cut.
Who did it? Add byWe had everything fixed by people who knew the job.
Bad things tooHe had his phone stolen. He didn't want that!
QuestionsWhat do you have done instead of doing it yourself?I have my hair cut every month.

5Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idioma piece of cake

something that is very easy to do

The test was a piece of cake. I finished in ten minutes.
proverbIf you want something done right, do it yourself.

Other people may not do a job as well as you want, so sometimes it is better to do it yourself.

My brother never cleans the car properly. If you want something done right, do it yourself.
phrasesort out

to solve a problem or put something right

There's a problem with my bank card, but I'll sort it out tomorrow.

professionaldone well, like the work of an expert
paintera person whose job is to paint walls and buildings
noticesee something and pay attention to it
exactlyno more and no less

Starting Your Own Business

Sara and Adam talk to a guest they know very well, Omar, about his first six months as a business owner.

Follow a podcast interviewTalk about starting a businessUse have and get something done

1Before you listen

Would you like to start your own business one day? What kind?

What do you think is the hardest part of starting a business?

2Listen and read The Future Vision Podcast · Episode 18

Hosts: Sara and Adam · Guest: Omar, who started a phone repair and app company
00:05AADAMWelcome back to The Future Vision Podcast. I'm Adam.
00:08SSARAAnd I'm Sara. Today's guest is someone we know very well. He started his own company six months ago. Welcome, Omar!
00:16OOMARThanks. It's strange to be on this side of the microphone.
00:20AADAMSo, Omar, why did you decide to be your own boss?
00:24OOMARI worked for a big company for a year, and I loved it. That's where I learned the ropes. But I always wanted to build something of my own.

01:55AADAMThat's exciting. Omar, thank you for coming.

Where did he learn the ropes?At a big company, where he worked for a year.

Who designed the logo?A student at the art college.

What did Omar learn about getting things done?It's cheaper to get things done by experts than to do them badly.

4Idioms, proverbs and phrases

phrasebe your own boss

to work for yourself and not for a company

My uncle left his job to be his own boss. Now he has a small shop.
idiomlearn the ropes

to learn the basic things you need to know to do a job

In my first month at the bank, I was still learning the ropes.

5New words

microphonea machine that you speak into to record your voice
accountsthe records of the money a business gets and spends
accountanta person whose job is to keep accounts

ADVANCED 2Unit 4 · Lesson 9
Story · Lesson 9

Who Ate the Cake?

A birthday cake disappears from the institute, and everyone is a suspect. Read the story, then read it from Mr. Ali's point of view.

Report what people said with reporting verbsUse the right pattern after each verbTell a funny mystery

1The story

It was almost Mr. Ali's sixtieth birthday, and his students had planned a surprise. On Wednesday afternoon, Huda bought a big chocolate cake from the best bakery in town and hid it in the fridge in the teachers' room. The party was going to be on Thursday morning, before the first class, and everyone promised to keep it a secret.

On Thursday, Huda opened the fridge. The cake was gone. "Somebody has taken it!" she cried. Within minutes, the whole class was in the teachers' room, and everyone was looking at everyone else.

Omar looked at Adam. "You were here late last night," he said. Adam denied going anywhere near the fridge. "I was only printing the birthday card," he said. Then Sara accused Omar of eating it, because there was chocolate on his shirt. "You've been caught red-handed!" she said. Omar admitted eating chocolate, but only a chocolate bar from the shop. "I refuse to be blamed for a crime I didn't commit," he said dramatically.

Huda was close to tears. Sara, practical as always, suggested checking the security camera in the corridor. The guard agreed to show them the video, but he warned them not to expect much. "That camera is older than I am," he said.

They watched in silence. At 9:40 the night before, a figure walked into the teachers' room and came out carrying a large white box. The picture wasn't clear, but the walk was. Everyone knew that slow, careful walk. The thief turned out to be Mr. Ali himself.

At that moment, the door opened, and Mr. Ali came in, carrying the box. "Good morning," he said. "I found this in the fridge last night. There was no name on it, and the cleaners empty the fridge on Thursdays, so I took it home to keep it safe." Then he opened the box and read the words on top: Happy Birthday, Mr. Ali. He laughed so much that he had to sit down.

He apologized for spoiling the surprise, and the students insisted on having the party anyway. "Well," said Mr. Ali, "don't judge a book by its cover. I looked like a thief, and so did Omar." As for Omar, everyone agreed that he still owed them a chocolate bar.

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Whose birthday was it?Mr. Ali's. It was almost his sixtieth.
2
Where did Huda hide the cake?In the fridge in the teachers' room.
3
When was the party going to be?On Thursday morning, before the first class.
4
What had everyone promised?To keep it a secret.
5
What did Adam deny?Going anywhere near the fridge.
6
Why did Sara accuse Omar?Because there was chocolate on his shirt.
7
What did Omar admit?Eating a chocolate bar from the shop.
8
What did Sara suggest?Checking the security camera in the corridor.
9
What did the guard warn them?Not to expect much, because the camera was old.
10
What did the video show?A figure carrying a large white box out of the teachers' room.
11
Why did Mr. Ali take the box home?There was no name on it, and the cleaners empty the fridge on Thursdays.
12
What did the students insist on?Having the party anyway.

3Point of view Now Mr. Ali tells it.

MA

On Wednesday night, I stayed late to mark exams. Before I left, I opened the fridge and found a big white box with no name on it. The cleaners empty the fridge on Thursdays, so I decided to take it home and keep it safe. I didn't even look inside.

The next morning, I walked into the teachers' room with the box and found my whole class there. They looked at me as if I were a criminal, and poor Huda looked as if she had been crying.

Then I opened the box and read the words on the cake. I laughed until I had to sit down. I apologized for spoiling their surprise, and I promised to look inside every box before I take it home.

Later, Sara told me the whole story. Adam had denied going near the fridge, and Omar had been accused of eating the cake. Omar still insists on telling everyone that he is innocent. I believe him. Mostly.

4What did you learn?

You learned reporting verbs.

When we report what people said, we often choose a verb that shows what they meant, a promise, a warning, or an apology. Each verb has its own pattern.

PatternExample
to do · promise, agree, refuse, offerEveryone promised to keep it a secret.
someone (not) to do · warn, advise, ask, tellHe warned them not to expect much.
-ing · deny, admit, suggestAdam denied going near the fridge.
someone of / for -ing · accuse, blameSara accused Omar of eating it.
for / on -ing · apologize for, insist onHe apologized for spoiling the surprise.
suggest + -ingSara suggested checking the camera. Not: suggested to check.
Negative: not before to or -ingHe warned them not to expect much. He admitted not knowing.
They say more than said"It wasn't me!" He denied doing it. "I'll help." He offered to help.
QuestionsWhat have you promised to do this week?I've promised to help my brother with his homework.

5Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idiombe caught red-handed

to be found while you are doing something wrong

The boy was caught red-handed with his hand in the cookie jar.
phraseturn out

to be found to be true in the end, often as a surprise

The exam turned out to be easier than we expected.
proverbDon't judge a book by its cover.

Don't decide what someone or something is like only from the way they look.

The restaurant looked old, but the food was wonderful. Don't judge a book by its cover.

6New words

bakerya shop that makes and sells bread and cakes
blamedsaid to be the person who did something wrong
dramaticallyin a way that is meant to impress people, like an actor
corridora long, narrow passage inside a building
figurethe shape of a person you can't see clearly
owedhad to give something back to someone

Police Warn of Phone Scam

Read a news report about a crime, and notice how reporters use verbs like warn, admit, and deny.

Read a crime reportFind who, what, where, when, and whyNotice reporting verbs in the news

1Read the article

The Daily NileMonday, March 9

Police Warn Public About Text Message Scam

Criminals are sending messages that look as if they come from banks, and dozens of people have already lost money.

By our crime reporter

Police in Khartoum have warned the public not to share bank codes with anyone, after dozens of people lost money to a new text message scam this month.

The messages look as if they come from a real bank. They tell people that they have won a prize, or that their account will be closed, and they ask them to send a secret code. "It sounded too good to be true, and it was," said one victim, a teacher who lost two months' salary. She admitted sending the code without thinking.

“It sounded too good to be true, and it was.”A teacher who lost two months' salary

A police spokesperson explained that the criminals often call after sending the message, pretending to be bank staff. "They are polite, they know your name, and they sound very professional," she said. "That's why so many people fall for it."

Banks have promised to return money to some of the victims, but they have advised customers to check every message carefully. "We will never ask you for a code by phone or text," said a manager at one bank.

One man was arrested last week, but he denied being part of the group. Police have asked anyone who receives a strange message to report it, and they have suggested calling the bank directly, using the number on the back of the card.

2The five key facts

Who?criminals pretending to be bank staff
What?a text message scam
Where?Khartoum
When?this month
Why?to steal money with secret bank codes

3Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
What have police warned the public not to do?Share bank codes with anyone.
2
What do the messages tell people?That they have won a prize, or that their account will be closed.
3
What did the teacher admit?Sending the code without thinking.
4
How do the criminals sound on the phone?Polite and very professional.
5
What have the banks promised?To return money to some of the victims.
6
What did the arrested man deny?Being part of the group.
7
What have police suggested?Calling the bank directly, using the number on the back of the card.

4Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idiomtoo good to be true

so good that it is probably not real

A new phone for only ten pounds? It's too good to be true.
phrasefall for something

to believe a trick or a lie

He told me the shop was giving away free cars, but I didn't fall for it.

5New words

scama clever trick to steal money
prizesomething you get when you win
victima person who is hurt or cheated by a crime
spokespersona person who speaks to the public for a group
criminalspeople who break the law
arrestedtaken away by the police

The Team Meeting

Making suggestions, disagreeing politely, and agreeing on a plan

Make and answer suggestionsDisagree politelySum up what people said

1Read the conversation

Sara leads a meeting with two engineers from her team, Tarig and Mona. Two more villages have asked for solar pumps.
SSARAOK, everyone. The pump near Kassala is working well, and two more villages have asked for one. We need a plan. Any ideas?
TTARIGI suggest starting with the bigger village. More people need the water there.
MOMONAI see your point, but the road to that village is closed in the rainy season. If we start there, we could lose two months.
TTARIGThat's true. I hadn't thought of that.
SSARAWhat if we start with the smaller village now and do the bigger one after the rains?
MOMONAThat makes sense. But we'll need more solar panels, and the budget is tight.
TTARIGCould we ask the university for help? They promised to support projects like ours.
SSARAGood idea. Mona, could you come up with a list of everything we need by Thursday?
MOMONASure. I'll send it to everyone on Thursday morning.
SSARAGreat. So, Tarig suggested asking the university, Mona agreed to make the list, and we'll start with the small village. Are we all on the same page?

2Useful phrases

Open the meeting

We need a plan. Any ideas?

Make a suggestion

I suggest starting with the bigger village.
What if we start with the smaller village?

Disagree politely

I see your point, but…

Agree

That's true.
That makes sense.

Give someone a task

Could you come up with a list by Thursday?

Sum up

So, Tarig suggested asking the university, and Mona agreed to make the list.

3Idioms, proverbs and phrases

phrasecome up with

to think of an idea, a plan, or an answer

We need to come up with a name for our new shop.
idiombe on the same page

to agree about a plan and understand it in the same way

Before we start, let's make sure we're all on the same page.

4New words

Story · Lesson 12

Adam Flies Alone

Six months after his first lesson, Adam is told that today he will fly with nobody next to him. Read the story, then read it from his instructor's point of view.

Give emphasis to what matters mostUse what clauses and it was … thatDescribe an important moment

1The story

Six months after his first lesson, Adam arrived at the flying school on a calm Tuesday morning. Captain Nour was waiting by the plane, as usual. But this time, she didn't climb in. "Today," she said, "you're going up alone."

Adam had imagined this moment a thousand times, but now that it had come, he had butterflies in his stomach. "Are you sure?" he asked. Captain Nour smiled. "What you need now is confidence, not more lessons. It's your hands that know how to fly, not mine."

He did his checks slowly and carefully, twice. Then he called the tower, and the voice on the radio said, "Cleared for take-off." The plane rolled down the runway, faster and faster, and then the ground fell away.

The first thing he noticed was the silence. There was nobody next to him, and no calm voice saying, "Gently." For a moment, his hands shook. Then he remembered the years of saving, the long nights reading about planes, and his grandfather's favorite words. "Where there's a will, there's a way." He took a deep breath and pulled himself together.

He flew one circle around the airfield. The Nile was shining below, just like on his first day, but this time, the sky was all his. When he landed, Captain Nour was clapping. Behind her, holding a sign that said WELL DONE, CAPTAIN ADAM, were Sara, Omar, and Huda. This time, Omar had checked every letter.

That evening, at the café, Sara asked him how it felt. Adam thought for a moment. "What I remember most is the silence," he said. "It was at that moment that I understood I was really a pilot."

"And how did you know we would be there?" asked Huda. "I didn't," said Adam. "But I think I know who told you. It was my grandfather, wasn't it?" Sara smiled. "Captain Nour told him yesterday, and he couldn't keep the secret for an hour."

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
When did Adam fly alone?Six months after his first lesson.
2
What did Captain Nour say?Today, you're going up alone.
3
How did Adam feel?He had butterflies in his stomach.
4
What did Captain Nour say he needed now?Confidence, not more lessons.
5
How many times did he do his checks?Twice.
6
What did the voice on the radio say?Cleared for take-off.
7
What was the first thing he noticed?The silence.
8
What were his grandfather's favorite words?Where there's a will, there's a way.
9
What did the sign say?WELL DONE, CAPTAIN ADAM.
10
What does Adam remember most?The silence.
11
When did he understand that he was really a pilot?At that moment, in the silence.
12
Who told the friends to come?Adam's grandfather.

3Point of view Now Captain Nour tells it.

CN

What I love most about my job is the day a student flies alone. I have seen it many times, and it still makes me nervous.

Adam was ready weeks ago, but he didn't know it. It was his confidence that needed more time, not his flying. So last Tuesday, I simply told him that he was going alone.

From the ground, I watched every second. His take-off was good, and his landing was even better. What surprised me was how calm he looked when he climbed out.

Of course, I had told his grandfather the day before. It was the only secret I have ever shared with a student's family, and I don't regret it.

4What did you learn?

You learned cleft sentences.

We use them to give emphasis, to point at the most important part of what we say.

Normal sentenceWith emphasis
I remember the silence most.What I remember most is the silence.
You need confidence now.What you need now is confidence.
I understood it at that moment.It was at that moment that I understood.
My grandfather told you.It was my grandfather who told you.
What … is / was …What I need is a holiday. What surprised me was his calm.
It is / It was … that / who …It was Sara who found the answer.
Say it: stress the key wordsIt was MY grandfather who told you.
QuestionsWhat do you like most about learning English?What I like most is the stories.

5Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idiomhave butterflies in your stomach

to feel very nervous before you do something

I always have butterflies in my stomach before an exam.
proverbWhere there's a will, there's a way.

If you really want to do something, you will find a way to do it.

He had no money for university, so he worked and saved. Where there's a will, there's a way.
phrasepull yourself together

to control your feelings and become calm again

She was crying, but she pulled herself together and finished her speech.

6New words

calmquiet and not nervous
confidencethe feeling that you can do something well
towerthe tall building at an airport where people tell pilots what to do
clearedallowed to do something
airfielda small airport
regretfeel sorry about something you did

Tell Me About a Time When…

Answering harder interview questions with examples from your life

Answer questions with real examplesGive emphasis to your strengthsTalk about a mistake and what you learned

1Read the conversation

Adam has an interview for a cadet program at an airline. Ms. Salma, a senior captain, is interviewing him.
MSMS. SALMAGood morning, Adam. Thank you for coming. Let's start. Why do you want to fly for an airline?
AADAMWhat I love most about flying is the responsibility. In a plane, every decision matters, and I want a job where people can trust me.
MSMS. SALMATell me about a time when you had to think on your feet.
AADAMLast month, during a training flight, my radio stopped working. It was then that I remembered the light signals from the tower. I followed them, and I landed safely.
MSMS. SALMAThat's impressive. How do you work under pressure?
AADAMI stay calm and follow my checklist. What helps me most is planning. If I've prepared well, I don't panic.
MSMS. SALMATell me about a time when you made a mistake.
AADAMIn my third lesson, I forgot one check before take-off, and my instructor noticed. It was that day that I started writing every check on a card. I've never forgotten one since.
MSMS. SALMAGood. One last question. Why should we choose you?
AADAMBecause I'm careful, I'm calm, and I never stop learning. And it's the pilots who never stop learning who become the best captains.

2Useful phrases

Say why you want the job

What I love most about flying is the responsibility.

Answer: Tell me about a time when…

Last month, during a training flight, my radio stopped working.

Say what you did

It was then that I remembered the light signals.

Talk about pressure

I stay calm and follow my checklist.

Learn from a mistake

It was that day that I started writing every check on a card.

Sell yourself

I'm careful, I'm calm, and I never stop learning.

3Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idiomthink on your feet

to make good decisions quickly, without time to plan

When the lights went out during her talk, she had to think on her feet.
phrasework under pressure

to do your work well when you have very little time or a lot of stress

Nurses often have to work under pressure.

4New words

cadeta young person who is training for a job such as pilot
responsibilitya duty to take care of something or someone
signalslights or sounds that give a message
impressivevery good, in a way that you admire
checklista list of things you must check or do
panicsuddenly feel so afraid that you can't think clearly
